body:
## Summary

`scripts/publish-retry.mjs` decides whether a failed `npm publish` still means
"this version is on the registry" by matching the output against:

```js
const ALREADY_PUBLISHED_PATTERNS = [
  'epublishconflict',
  'cannot publish over the previously published version',
  'cannot publish over previously published version',
  'you cannot publish over the previously published versions',
  'already published',
];
```

npm has a second wording for the same situation that none of these match:

```
npm error code E409
npm error 409 Conflict - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg> - Cannot publish over previously staged version "0.20.1"
```

`staged`, not `published`, and the code is `E409`, not `EPUBLISHCONFLICT`. This
is what the registry returns when the tarball for the version has been accepted
but the version is not yet visible on the public read path — exactly the window
the retry loop exists to ride out.

The consequence is the inverse of the bug the retry loop was written for: the
release *succeeded*, the version exists, and the workflow fails anyway. A
maintainer then sees a red release job for a package that is on npm, and any
subsequent rerun hits the same E409 forever, because the conflict is permanent
once the version is staged.

## Real occurrence

From `link-foundation/command-stream` CI (run 33897699209, JavaScript release
job):

```
🦋  error an error occurred while publishing command-stream: E409 409 Conflict - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/command-stream - Cannot publish over previously staged version "0.20.0".
```

and on the following release attempt, with `0.20.1`:

```
npm error code E409
npm error 409 Conflict - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/command-stream - Cannot publish over previously staged version "0.20.1"
```

Both versions were live on npm at the time the job was marked failed.

## Reproducible example

The classifier is pure, so the defect reproduces without touching a registry:

```js
import { isAlreadyPublishedError } from './scripts/publish-retry.mjs';

const staged =
  'npm error code E409\n' +
  'npm error 409 Conflict - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/pkg - ' +
  'Cannot publish over previously staged version "0.20.1"';

const published =
  'npm error code EPUBLISHCONFLICT\n' +
  'npm error Cannot publish over previously published version "0.20.1"';

console.log('staged   :', isAlreadyPublishedError(staged));    // false  ← bug
console.log('published:', isAlreadyPublishedError(published)); // true
```

Both inputs describe a version that is present on the registry; only the second
is recognised.

## Workaround

Re-running does not help — the conflict is permanent. The manual workaround is
to confirm the version with `npm view <pkg>@<version> version` and dismiss the
red job by hand, which is precisely the manual step this script removes for the
other wording.

## Suggested fix

Add the staged wordings to the pattern list:

```js
const ALREADY_PUBLISHED_PATTERNS = [
  'epublishconflict',
  'cannot publish over the previously published version',
  'cannot publish over previously published version',
  'you cannot publish over the previously published versions',
  // npm returns E409 with this wording while the version is accepted but not
  // yet visible on the public read path — the same "it is already there"
  // situation the patterns above describe, and the window this retry loop
  // exists to ride out.
  'cannot publish over the previously staged version',
  'cannot publish over previously staged version',
  'previously staged version',
  'already published',
];
```

Keeping the bare `'previously staged version'` entry alongside the two full
sentences means a future rewording of the prefix by npm still matches.

Two notes on the surrounding code:

- The message logged on this branch reads "already published"; "already
  published or staged" describes both cases, and makes the log match the
  registry's own wording when a maintainer greps for it.
- Matching the message is inherently fragile. The classification is only used
  to decide whether to *verify* against the registry, and the verification is
  the actual proof, so the failure mode of a wrong match is bounded — but it is
  worth a comment saying so, otherwise the next reader assumes the string list
  is authoritative.

A regression test over `isAlreadyPublishedError` with both wordings pins this
cheaply, since the function takes a string and returns a boolean.

## Context

Found while auditing CI for false positives and false negatives in
`link-foundation/command-stream` (link-foundation/command-stream#199), where
this exact E409 turned two successful npm releases into failed jobs. The fix
above is applied there in `js/scripts/publish-retry.mjs`.
title: publish-retry: E409 "Cannot publish over previously staged version" is not recognised as already-published, so a successful release fails the job
